DC-01.reason: Two randomized studies show herbicide raised native cover in most site-years, with two non-significant 1996 cohorts.

DC-02.reason: Across four randomized trials fertilization usually increased seedling height/diameter, but responses were species- and season-dependent (several nulls for jack pine, tamarack, first-season height).

DC-03.reason: Five independent randomized trials consistently show scarification increased conifer height vs unscarified controls (one null height-increment contrast); double- vs single-pass and scarified+fertilized contrasts are not clean tests.

DC-04.reason: Two studies (quasi-experimental/longitudinal) report rewetting reduced tree cover/biomass and shrub cover, though shrub biomass may rebound over time.

DC-05.reason: Two randomized experiments at three sites consistently show liming raised soil pH vs unlimed controls.

DC-06.reason: Liming increased sugar maple sapling growth but had no effect on beech, overall height, or spruce height at most sites.

DC-07.reason: Single quasi-experimental study: water table rose post-rewetting in most transects near dams, but not in a distant transect (one even deeper).

DC-08.reason: One quasi-experimental grazed-vs-ungrazed comparison found lower litter mass and standing crop under grazing (associational).

DC-09.reason: One study at one of several sites found lower exotic grass abundance with grass-specific herbicide, compared only against other treatments.

DC-10.reason: One randomized study found burn treatments (combined with glyphosate) lowered non-native forb and grass cover, so burning's effect is confounded with herbicide.

DC-11.reason: Before-after comparisons without controls show no significant change for most metals, but Cu and Hg in sediment decreased and Hg/Zn in crabs differed in some years.

DC-12.reason: Two randomized studies found one-time mulching did not change native seedling densities; the 'increase' edge's sentence is about exotic species and does not support it.

DC-13.reason: One study found phenol levels generally higher in browsed (outside-exclosure) and heavily browsed saplings, with exceptions; associational; tannin edge's sentence only reports phenols.

DC-14.reason: One randomized trial found weed removal increased seedling diameter and biomass, though effects varied by site and component.

DC-15.reason: Removing competing vegetation increased seedling diameter and biomass in one randomized trial, implying competition reduces conifer growth.

DC-16.reason: Edge encodes that unsheltered trees were browsed more, implying shelters reduce browsing, but the sentence mainly reports a species effect among unprotected trees.

DC-17.reason: One exclosure study found saplings taller inside than outside moose exclosures (associational, quasi-experimental).

DC-18.reason: One randomized trial found exponential fertilization increased seedling height, diameter and biomass relative to conventional fertilization.

DC-19.reason: Mulch had only a borderline (p=0.06) effect on species assemblages in a single sampling date.

DC-20.reason: A cross-sectional chronosequence found soil exchangeable K remained stable after forest conversion to fallow fields.

DC-21.reason: Movement models show bears moving closer to or further from seismic lines depending on sex, season, landcover and line vegetation height.

DC-22.reason: One randomized experiment found base saturation 1.4-3x higher in limed soils vs controls at two depths.

DC-23.reason: Liming increased sugar maple sapling basal area and biomass growth but had no effect on American beech or overall height growth.

DC-29.reason: Only edge describes fertilization moderating the scarification effect on GLD, not fertilization's direct effect.

DC-30.reason: Randomized trial: total basal area was highest in uncut controls and lower in all cutting treatments (edge encoding of 'increased variation' contradicts sentence); other edges concern stock quality, not basal area.

DC-31.reason: Effects are interaction-dependent: scarification reduced conifer density in some cutting treatments, while birch/other hardwood/non-commercial densities became higher in raked plots after 15 years.
